Proving the Fundamental Theorem

Lesson text (draft) · Teacher's sheet

The auditor’s question

At the end of the last review, someone from the research team asked whether you could prove the fundamental theorem of lesson 6a, both directions, with the exact rates. That question now has a deadline. The interval filter of lesson 6a, which scores every message with the spam score, a number between 0 and 1, and labels it junk when the score falls inside an interval it has learned, is about to get its first outside audit. The class of intervals has VC dimension 2 (it can label two messages every possible way, but never three), and the certificate your team filed back then rests on one sentence from lesson 6a: the fundamental theorem of statistical learning, quantitative version. Write ddd for the VC dimension, ε\varepsilonε for the accuracy you ask for and δ\deltaδ for the chance you allow the guarantee to fail. The theorem says the number of labels a class needs grows like d+log⁡(1/δ)d + \log(1/\delta)d+log(1/δ) over ε2\varepsilon^2ε2 when labels are noisy, and roughly like dlog⁡(1/ε)+log⁡(1/δ)d \log(1/\varepsilon) + \log(1/\delta)dlog(1/ε)+log(1/δ) over ε\varepsilonε when some interval is perfect.

The certificate has two lines. The clean line covers the mailboxes where one interval really does separate junk from keep. The noisy line covers the shared mailboxes, where users disagree and no interval is perfect. Both promise a filter within ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1 of the best possible, with confidence 1−δ=0.951 - \delta = 0.951−δ=0.95, and both budgets were computed by plugging the numbers into the theorem’s shapes:

from math import log

d, eps, delta = 2, 0.1, 0.05
agnostic_shape = (d + log(1 / delta)) / eps ** 2
realizable_shape = (d * log(1 / eps) + log(1 / delta)) / eps
print(round(agnostic_shape), round(realizable_shape))

It prints 500 76. So the certificate says: 76 labels for the clean line, 500 for the noisy line.

The auditor reads it twice and puts down her pen. “Lesson 6a says there are constants C1C_1C1​ and C2C_2C2​ that make this true. You used 1 for both. Where is the proof that 1 works? And the lower constant: how do you know a smaller budget could not have done the job? If you can’t show me a floor and a ceiling, this certificate is a guess with a theorem’s name on it.”

She is right, and it is a little embarrassing. Lesson 6a stated the quantitative theorem and promised the proof for later. Your team has been quoting its rates ever since without anyone checking where they come from. This lesson pays that debt and answers the research team’s question. We will prove three things, each with explicit constants:

  1. The ceiling with noisy labels: enough labels, of order (dlog⁡(1/ε)+log⁡(1/δ))/ε2(d \log(1/\varepsilon) + \log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2(dlog(1/ε)+log(1/δ))/ε2, make ERM (lesson 2’s learner that returns a hypothesis with the smallest empirical risk) succeed for every distribution.
  2. The floor with noisy labels: fewer than about (d+log⁡(1/δ))/ε2(d + \log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2(d+log(1/δ))/ε2 labels make every learner fail on some distribution.
  3. The ceiling with clean labels: when some hypothesis is perfect, order (dlog⁡(1/ε)+log⁡(1/δ))/ε(d \log(1/\varepsilon) + \log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon(dlog(1/ε)+log(1/δ))/ε labels are enough, the faster 1/ε1/\varepsilon1/ε rate.

By the end you will rewrite both lines of the certificate with numbers you can defend, and you will see why no budget below the floor could ever be defended at all.

What exactly must be proved

Let’s set out the vocabulary, since every step below leans on it.

A hypothesis class H\mathcal HH is a set of hypotheses h:X→{0,1}h: \mathcal X \to \{0, 1\}h:X→{0,1}, where X\mathcal XX is the domain (here, spam scores) and the label 1 means junk. Its VC dimension ddd (lesson 6a) is the size of the largest set CCC of messages that H\mathcal HH shatters, that is, labels in all 2∣C∣2^{|C|}2∣C∣ possible ways, where ∣C∣|C|∣C∣ is the number of messages in CCC. For intervals, d=2d = 2d=2: any two scores can be labelled every way, but no three can, since “junk, keep, junk” would need a gap inside an interval.

A training sequence S=(z1,…,zm)S = (z_1, \dots, z_m)S=(z1​,…,zm​) is mmm examples zi=(xi,yi)z_i = (x_i, y_i)zi​=(xi​,yi​) drawn i.i.d. from a distribution D\mathcal DD over messages and labels; we write S∼DmS \sim \mathcal D^mS∼Dm. The true risk LD(h)L_{\mathcal D}(h)LD​(h) is the chance that hhh mislabels a fresh example, and the empirical risk LS(h)L_S(h)LS​(h) is the fraction of SSS that hhh gets wrong. The best in the class is min⁡h∈HLD(h)\min_{h \in \mathcal H} L_{\mathcal D}(h)minh∈H​LD​(h), the smallest true risk any hypothesis in H\mathcal HH can reach. When a learner AAA returns A(S)A(S)A(S), the amount by which it falls short of the best in the class,

LD(A(S))−min⁡h∈HLD(h),L_{\mathcal D}(A(S)) - \min_{h \in \mathcal H} L_{\mathcal D}(h),LD​(A(S))−h∈Hmin​LD​(h),

is its estimation error, as in lesson 5. Here A(S)A(S)A(S) is the hypothesis the learner returns on SSS, LD(A(S))L_{\mathcal D}(A(S))LD​(A(S)) is its true risk, and the min⁡\minmin is the best in the class. In plain words: how much worse the learner’s hypothesis is than the best one it could have picked. If the best interval errs on 12% of noisy mail and the learner’s errs on 15%, the estimation error is 0.03. A run is a miss when the estimation error exceeds ε\varepsilonε.

A class is agnostic PAC learnable (lesson 3) when some learner, given enough examples, avoids a miss with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, for every distribution D\mathcal DD. The sample complexity mH(ε,δ)m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta)mH​(ε,δ) is the smallest number of examples for which some learner can promise this. When some hypothesis has true risk 0, the setting is realizable, and the promise is simply LD(A(S))≤εL_{\mathcal D}(A(S)) \le \varepsilonLD​(A(S))≤ε.

Two kinds of statement bracket the sample complexity, and it helps to name them now.

  • A ceiling says: this many examples are enough, for one particular learner. It is an upper bound on mH(ε,δ)m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta)mH​(ε,δ).
  • A floor says: with fewer examples than this, every learner misses too often on some distribution. It is a lower bound on mH(ε,δ)m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta)mH​(ε,δ).

A ceiling is proved by building a learner and analysing it. A floor is harder in spirit: you must defeat all learners at once, including ones nobody has invented yet. Lesson 5 did exactly this for the No-Free-Lunch theorem, and we will borrow its trick.

Throughout, log⁡\loglog is the natural logarithm, and e≈2.718e \approx 2.718e≈2.718 is its base.

[diagram:ceiling-floor: built on the lesson page]

The picture above is the certificate’s noisy line on a number line of budgets. Below the floor, no learner can succeed, whatever it does. Above the ceiling, ERM is proved to succeed. In between lies a band where nobody has a proof either way, and an auditor cannot sign there. The whole lesson is about pinning those two fences down.

The ceiling with noisy labels

### The plan, in words

Lesson 4 gave the strategy. Call a training sequence ε\varepsilonε-representative when every hypothesis in the class has empirical risk within ε\varepsilonε of its true risk. If SSS is ε/2\varepsilon/2ε/2-representative, then ERM, which returns a hypothesis with the smallest empirical risk, has estimation error at most ε\varepsilonε. Write hSh_ShS​ for ERM’s output and h⋆h^\starh⋆ for the best hypothesis in the class; then LD(hS)≤LS(hS)+ε/2≤LS(h⋆)+ε/2≤LD(h⋆)+εL_{\mathcal D}(h_S) \le L_S(h_S) + \varepsilon/2 \le L_S(h^\star) + \varepsilon/2 \le L_{\mathcal D}(h^\star) + \varepsilonLD​(hS​)≤LS​(hS​)+ε/2≤LS​(h⋆)+ε/2≤LD​(h⋆)+ε, where the outer steps are representativeness and the middle one is ERM picking the lowest empirical risk. So we need one thing: a number of examples that makes SSS representative with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ.

Lesson 26 built the tools for this: the Rademacher complexity, McDiarmid’s inequality to turn it into a guarantee, and Massart’s lemma to compute it for a finite set. Let’s recall the three facts we need before we use them.

### Three facts from lesson 26

Fix the training sequence and line up, for each hypothesis, its loss vector: entry iii is its loss on example iii, 1 for a mistake and 0 otherwise. Collect these vectors in a set A⊆RmA \subseteq \mathbb R^mA⊆Rm, the set of real vectors of length mmm. The random signs σ1,…,σm\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_mσ1​,…,σm​ are independent, each +1+1+1 or −1-1−1 with chance one half, the Rademacher variables of lesson 26. The Rademacher complexity of AAA is

R(A)=1m Eσ[sup⁡a∈A∑i=1mσiai].R(A) = \frac{1}{m} \, \mathbb E_{\sigma} \left[ \sup_{a \in A} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sigma_i a_i \right].R(A)=m1​Eσ​[a∈Asup​i=1∑m​σi​ai​].

From the inside out:

  • aia_iai​ is coordinate iii of a vector aaa, the loss of one hypothesis on example iii.
  • ∑i=1mσiai\sum_{i=1}^{m} \sigma_i a_i∑i=1m​σi​ai​ adds up the losses, each with a random sign. Think of the signs as splitting the examples into two random halves, and the sum as “mistakes on the +++ half minus mistakes on the −-− half”; or think of them as random fake labels, pure noise.
  • sup⁡a∈A\sup_{a \in A}supa∈A​ (the supremum, which for a finite set is just the maximum) picks the vector that makes that sum as large as possible: the hypothesis that best fits this noise.
  • Eσ\mathbb E_{\sigma}Eσ​ averages over all 2m2^m2m equally likely sign vectors, and 1m\frac{1}{m}m1​ turns the total into a per-example rate.

In plain words: how well, on average, the class’s losses can fit pure noise on these very messages. A class that can fit any noise is rich enough to fit the accidents of your training sequence too; a class that cannot is safe. On one example, with A={(0),(1)}A = \{(0), (1)\}A={(0),(1)}, the sign is +1+1+1 half the time (the best vector scores 1) and −1-1−1 half the time (the best vector, (0)(0)(0), scores 0), so R(A)=12R(A) = \tfrac12R(A)=21​. The snippet in Step 2 below computes this average exactly, by trying every sign vector.

The second fact, lesson 26’s Rademacher generalization bound, turns this into a guarantee. Let ℓ(h,z)\ell(h, z)ℓ(h,z) be the loss of hhh on example zzz, and suppose ∣ℓ(h,z)∣≤c|\ell(h, z)| \le c∣ℓ(h,z)∣≤c for every hhh and zzz, where the bars are absolute value. Write ℓ∘H∘S′\ell \circ \mathcal H \circ S'ℓ∘H∘S′ for the set of loss vectors on a sequence S′S'S′. Then, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over S∼DmS \sim \mathcal D^mS∼Dm, every h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H satisfies

LD(h)−LS(h)≤2 ES′∼Dm[R(ℓ∘H∘S′)]+c2log⁡(2/δ)m.L_{\mathcal D}(h) - L_S(h) \le 2 \, \mathbb E_{S' \sim \mathcal D^m} \left[ R(\ell \circ \mathcal H \circ S') \right] + c \sqrt{\frac{2 \log(2/\delta)}{m}}.LD​(h)−LS​(h)≤2ES′∼Dm​[R(ℓ∘H∘S′)]+cm2log(2/δ)​​.

Reading it: the left side is how much hypothesis hhh flatters itself on SSS, true risk minus empirical risk. On the right, S′S'S′ is another training sequence drawn from Dm\mathcal D^mDm, and ES′\mathbb E_{S'}ES′​ averages the Rademacher complexity of the loss vectors over all such sequences. The factor 2 comes from lesson 26’s symmetrization lemma (the ghost sample and the random signs), which bounds the average, over training sequences, of the worst self-flattery in the class. The last term is the price of confidence, and it comes from McDiarmid’s inequality: a function of mmm independent examples that no single example can move by more than c′c'c′ stays within c′mlog⁡(2/δ)/2c'\sqrt{m \log(2/\delta)/2}c′mlog(2/δ)/2​ of its average, except with probability δ\deltaδ. Changing one example moves every empirical risk, and so the worst self-flattery, by at most 2c/m2c/m2c/m; with c′=2c/mc' = 2c/mc′=2c/m the radius is exactly c2log⁡(2/δ)/mc\sqrt{2 \log(2/\delta)/m}c2log(2/δ)/m​. It shrinks like 1/m1/\sqrt m1/m​ and grows only with the log of 1/δ1/\delta1/δ. In plain words: no hypothesis can look better on the training sequence than it really is by more than twice the class’s average Rademacher complexity plus a small confidence term. With the 0-1 loss, c=1c = 1c=1; at m=10,000m = 10{,}000m=10,000 and δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05, the confidence term is 2log⁡40/10,000≈0.027\sqrt{2 \log 40 / 10{,}000} \approx 0.0272log40/10,000​≈0.027:

from math import log, sqrt

m, delta, c = 10_000, 0.05, 1
step = 2 * c / m
radius = step * sqrt(m * log(2 / delta) / 2)
term = c * sqrt(2 * log(2 / delta) / m)
print(round(radius, 4), round(term, 4))

It prints 0.0272 0.0272: McDiarmid’s radius with one example’s reach 2c/m2c/m2c/m is the bound’s confidence term.

The third fact, Massart’s lemma, bounds the Rademacher complexity of a finite set. If A={a1,…,aN}A = \{a_1, \dots, a_N\}A={a1​,…,aN​} has N≥2N \ge 2N≥2 vectors and aˉ=1N∑j=1Naj\bar a = \frac1N \sum_{j=1}^{N} a_jaˉ=N1​∑j=1N​aj​ is their average, then

R(A)≤max⁡a∈A∥a−aˉ∥ 2log⁡Nm.R(A) \le \max_{a \in A} \|a - \bar a\| \, \frac{\sqrt{2 \log N}}{m}.R(A)≤a∈Amax​∥a−aˉ∥m2logN​​.

Here ∥a−aˉ∥\|a - \bar a\|∥a−aˉ∥ is the Euclidean length of the vector from the average to aaa, the square root of the sum of its squared coordinates, and max⁡a∈A\max_{a \in A}maxa∈A​ takes the longest one, the set’s spread. In plain words: a finite set fits noise no better than its spread times 2log⁡N\sqrt{2\log N}2logN​, divided by mmm. The log is what makes this useful: a million hypotheses cost only 2log⁡106≈5.3\sqrt{2 \log 10^6} \approx 5.32log106​≈5.3. The Step 2 snippet checks it against the exact complexity.

Now we can follow the chain.

### Step 1: as many loss vectors as labellings

Take eight messages with scores 0,1,…,70, 1, \dots, 70,1,…,7 (only their order matters) and some noisy labels, say junk at positions 2, 3 and 5. Each interval labels the eight messages somehow, and comparing with the users’ labels turns that labelling into a mistake pattern. How many different mistake patterns can intervals produce? Before you count, notice something: if you know the users’ labels, the labelling and the mistake pattern determine each other. A mistake at position iii means “the opposite of yiy_iyi​”, no mistake means “the same as yiy_iyi​”. So there are exactly as many mistake patterns as labellings.

Formally, fix S=((x1,y1),…,(xm,ym))S = ((x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_m, y_m))S=((x1​,y1​),…,(xm​,ym​)) and let

A={(1[h(x1)≠y1],…,1[h(xm)≠ym]):h∈H}.A = \left\{ \left( \mathbb 1[h(x_1) \neq y_1], \dots, \mathbb 1[h(x_m) \neq y_m] \right) : h \in \mathcal H \right\}.A={(1[h(x1​)=y1​],…,1[h(xm​)=ym​]):h∈H}.

The indicator 1[⋅]\mathbb 1[\cdot]1[⋅] is 1 when the statement inside is true and 0 otherwise, so each coordinate is the 0-1 loss of hhh on one example. The braces collect one vector per hypothesis, and the colon reads “such that hhh ranges over H\mathcal HH”; two hypotheses with the same mistakes give the same vector, counted once. In plain words: AAA is the set of all mistake patterns the class can make on this training sequence. The map from labelling (h(x1),…,h(xm))(h(x_1), \dots, h(x_m))(h(x1​),…,h(xm​)) to mistake pattern flips coordinate iii exactly when yi=1y_i = 1yi​=1, and flipping twice undoes it, so the map is a bijection. Hence ∣A∣|A|∣A∣ equals the number of labellings the class produces on x1,…,xmx_1, \dots, x_mx1​,…,xm​, which is at most the growth function τH(m)\tau_{\mathcal H}(m)τH​(m) of lesson 6b, the largest number of labellings the class makes on any mmm messages. By Sauer’s lemma, for m≥dm \ge dm≥d,

∣A∣≤τH(m)≤(emd)d.|A| \le \tau_{\mathcal H}(m) \le \left( \frac{em}{d} \right)^d.∣A∣≤τH​(m)≤(dem​)d.

On the left, the number of mistake patterns; in the middle, the most labellings of any mmm messages; on the right, Sauer’s polynomial, em/dem/dem/d raised to the power ddd. In plain words: a class of VC dimension ddd makes at most about mdm^dmd mistake patterns, not 2m2^m2m. For intervals on eight messages, (4e)2≈118(4e)^2 \approx 118(4e)2≈118, against 28=2562^8 = 25628=256:

from math import e

m, d = 8, 2
y = (0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0)
cuts = [c - 0.5 for c in range(m + 1)]
H_C = {tuple(int(a < x < b) for x in range(m))
       for a in cuts for b in cuts if a <= b}
A = {tuple(int(h_i != y_i) for h_i, y_i in zip(h, y))
     for h in H_C}
print(len(H_C), len(A), round((e * m / d) ** d, 1))

It prints 37 37 118.2: 37 labellings, 37 mistake patterns, exactly as the bijection says, and Sauer’s bound sits comfortably above both.

### Step 2: Massart turns the count into a complexity

Every coordinate of a vector in AAA is 0 or 1, and every coordinate of the average aˉ\bar aaˉ lies between 0 and 1, so every coordinate of a−aˉa - \bar aa−aˉ lies between −1-1−1 and 111. Its square is at most 1, the sum of mmm such squares is at most mmm, and so ∥a−aˉ∥≤m\|a - \bar a\| \le \sqrt m∥a−aˉ∥≤m​. Massart’s lemma then gives

R(A)≤m⋅2log⁡∣A∣m=2log⁡∣A∣m≤2dlog⁡(em/d)m,R(A) \le \sqrt m \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2 \log |A|}}{m} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \log |A|}{m}} \le \sqrt{\frac{2 d \log(em/d)}{m}},R(A)≤m​⋅m2log∣A∣​​=m2log∣A∣​​≤m2dlog(em/d)​​,

where the last step puts in Step 1’s ∣A∣≤(em/d)d|A| \le (em/d)^d∣A∣≤(em/d)d, whose log is dlog⁡(em/d)d \log(em/d)dlog(em/d). In plain words: the class’s Rademacher complexity on any training sequence is at most the square root of 2dlog⁡(em/d)2d \log(em/d)2dlog(em/d) over mmm. It does not depend on which sequence we drew, so it also bounds the average ES′\mathbb E_{S'}ES′​ in the second fact.

Let’s check it by brute force on ten messages, where all 210=1,0242^{10} = 1{,}024210=1,024 sign vectors can be tried:

from itertools import product
from math import e, log, sqrt

m, d = 10, 2
y = (0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0)
cuts = [c - 0.5 for c in range(m + 1)]
H_C = {tuple(int(a < x < b) for x in range(m))
       for a in cuts for b in cuts if a <= b}
A = {tuple(int(h != t) for h, t in zip(h_c, y)) for h_c in H_C}
signs = list(product([-1, 1], repeat=m))
R = sum(max(sum(s * a for s, a in zip(sig, v)) for v in A)
        for sig in signs) / len(signs) / m
massart = sqrt(2 * log(len(A)) / m)
sauer = sqrt(2 * d * log(e * m / d) / m)
print(len(A), round(R, 3), round(massart, 3), round(sauer, 3))

It prints 56 0.308 0.897 1.022. The exact complexity is 0.308; Massart with the m\sqrt mm​ length gives 0.897, and Sauer’s count gives 1.022. Each step loosens the bound, which is the price of a proof that works for every class and every sequence. Ten messages is far too few for anything useful; the point is that the inequalities hold, and they shrink like log⁡m/m\sqrt{\log m / m}logm/m​.

### Step 3: both sides at once

Put Step 2 into the second fact with c=1c = 1c=1 and confidence δ/2\delta/2δ/2. Since 2x=4x2\sqrt{x} = \sqrt{4x}2x​=4x​, twice the complexity bound is 8dlog⁡(em/d)/m\sqrt{8 d \log(em/d)/m}8dlog(em/d)/m​, and with probability at least 1−δ/21 - \delta/21−δ/2, every hhh has

LD(h)−LS(h)≤8dlog⁡(em/d)m+2log⁡(4/δ)m.L_{\mathcal D}(h) - L_S(h) \le \sqrt{\frac{8 d \log(em/d)}{m}} + \sqrt{\frac{2 \log(4/\delta)}{m}}.LD​(h)−LS​(h)≤m8dlog(em/d)​​+m2log(4/δ)​​.

That is one side: no hypothesis looks much better on SSS than it is. We also need the other side, that none looks much worse. Here is the trick. Use the loss −ℓ-\ell−ℓ instead of ℓ\ellℓ. It is still bounded by c=1c = 1c=1 in absolute value, its true and empirical risks are −LD(h)-L_{\mathcal D}(h)−LD​(h) and −LS(h)-L_S(h)−LS​(h), and its loss vectors are −A-A−A. Flipping every vector does not change the Rademacher complexity, because σ\sigmaσ and −σ-\sigma−σ are equally likely, so R(−A)=R(A)R(-A) = R(A)R(−A)=R(A): lesson 26’s shift-and-scale rule with factor −1-1−1. The same argument, again at confidence δ/2\delta/2δ/2, gives the same bound for LS(h)−LD(h)L_S(h) - L_{\mathcal D}(h)LS​(h)−LD​(h).

Each of the two bounds fails with probability at most δ/2\delta/2δ/2. By the union bound (lesson 2: the chance that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their chances), at least one fails with probability at most δ\deltaδ. So with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, both hold, and every hhh has

∣LD(h)−LS(h)∣≤8dlog⁡(em/d)m+2log⁡(4/δ)m≤28dlog⁡(em/d)+2log⁡(4/δ)m.|L_{\mathcal D}(h) - L_S(h)| \le \sqrt{\frac{8 d \log(em/d)}{m}} + \sqrt{\frac{2 \log(4/\delta)}{m}} \le 2 \sqrt{\frac{8 d \log(em/d) + 2 \log(4/\delta)}{m}}.∣LD​(h)−LS​(h)∣≤m8dlog(em/d)​​+m2log(4/δ)​​≤2m8dlog(em/d)+2log(4/δ)​​.

The last step uses a+b≤2a+b\sqrt a + \sqrt b \le 2\sqrt{a + b}a​+b​≤2a+b​, which holds because each of a\sqrt aa​ and b\sqrt bb​ is at most a+b\sqrt{a + b}a+b​. The bars on the left are absolute value: the gap between true and empirical risk, whichever way it points. In plain words: with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, every interval’s training score is within this many points of its true score, all at once. Here is the right-hand side for intervals at δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05:

from math import e, log, sqrt

d, delta = 2, 0.05
def gap_bound(m):
    inside = 8 * d * log(e * m / d) + 2 * log(4 / delta)
    return 2 * sqrt(inside / m)
for m in (1_000, 10_000, 119_191, 547_743):
    print(m, round(gap_bound(m), 4))

It prints

1000 0.7048
10000 0.2538
119191 0.0821
547743 0.0405

At a thousand labels the bound is useless (0.70 allows almost any gap), at ten thousand it says 0.25, and only in the hundreds of thousands does it get below 0.05. The last two rows are no accident; the next step explains where they come from.

### Step 4: solving for mmm

We want the bound to be at most a target ε\varepsilonε. Squaring and rearranging, that is

mε24≥8dlog⁡(emd)+2log⁡(4δ).\frac{m \varepsilon^2}{4} \ge 8 d \log\left(\frac{em}{d}\right) + 2 \log\left(\frac{4}{\delta}\right).4mε2​≥8dlog(dem​)+2log(δ4​).

The trouble is that mmm appears on both sides, once inside a log. We need a way to pull it out, and a small lemma does it.

The log curve bends down, so it never rises above a straight line that touches it: at x=20x = 20x=20, log⁡20≈3.00\log 20 \approx 3.00log20≈3.00, while the line touching the curve at 777 has already climbed to log⁡7+20/7−1≈3.80\log 7 + 20/7 - 1 \approx 3.80log7+20/7−1≈3.80. A straight line in mmm is easy to solve for, so we swap the log for one.

The tangent-line lemma. For all x>0x > 0x>0 and t>0t > 0t>0, log⁡x≤log⁡t+xt−1\log x \le \log t + \frac{x}{t} - 1logx≤logt+tx​−1.

The right side is the tangent line to the log curve at the point ttt: a straight line with slope 1/t1/t1/t that touches the curve at x=tx = tx=t. In plain words: the log curve never rises above any of its tangent lines.

Proof. Let g(x)=log⁡t+x/t−1−log⁡xg(x) = \log t + x/t - 1 - \log xg(x)=logt+x/t−1−logx. Its derivative 1/t−1/x1/t - 1/x1/t−1/x is negative for x<tx < tx<t and positive for x>tx > tx>t, so ggg is smallest at x=tx = tx=t, where g(t)=log⁡t+1−1−log⁡t=0g(t) = \log t + 1 - 1 - \log t = 0g(t)=logt+1−1−logt=0. So g(x)≥0g(x) \ge 0g(x)≥0 everywhere. ■\blacksquare■

Now choose the tangent point cleverly. Apply the lemma with x=em/dx = em/dx=em/d and t=64e/ε2t = 64e/\varepsilon^2t=64e/ε2, and multiply by 8d8d8d:

8dlog⁡(emd)≤8dlog⁡(64eε2)+8d⋅emd⋅ε264e−8d=8dlog⁡(64ε2)+mε28.8d \log\left(\frac{em}{d}\right) \le 8d \log\left(\frac{64e}{\varepsilon^2}\right) + 8d \cdot \frac{em}{d} \cdot \frac{\varepsilon^2}{64 e} - 8d = 8d \log\left(\frac{64}{\varepsilon^2}\right) + \frac{m \varepsilon^2}{8}.8dlog(dem​)≤8dlog(ε264e​)+8d⋅dem​⋅64eε2​−8d=8dlog(ε264​)+8mε2​.

The ceiling for uniform convergence. Let H\mathcal HH have VC dimension d≥1d \ge 1d≥1. For every distribution D\mathcal DD, every ε,δ∈(0,1)\varepsilon, \delta \in (0, 1)ε,δ∈(0,1), and every

m≥64 dlog⁡(64/ε2)+16log⁡(4/δ)ε2,m \ge \frac{64 \, d \log(64/\varepsilon^2) + 16 \log(4/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2},m≥ε264dlog(64/ε2)+16log(4/δ)​,

a training sequence S∼DmS \sim \mathcal D^mS∼Dm is ε\varepsilonε-representative with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ.

Read it once more. The numerator has the VC dimension times a log of 1/ε1/\varepsilon1/ε, plus the log of 1/δ1/\delta1/δ; the whole is divided by ε2\varepsilon^2ε2. In plain words: about 64dlog⁡(64/ε2)+16log⁡(4/δ)64 d \log(64/\varepsilon^2) + 16\log(4/\delta)64dlog(64/ε2)+16log(4/δ) labels per unit of ε2\varepsilon^2ε2 make every hypothesis’s training score honest to within ε\varepsilonε. (The value of mmm is far above ddd, so Sauer’s form from Step 1 applies.)

To get the learning guarantee, remember that ERM needs representativeness at level ε/2\varepsilon/2ε/2. Putting ε/2\varepsilon/2ε/2 in place of ε\varepsilonε multiplies 64/ε264/\varepsilon^264/ε2 by 4 inside the log and the whole fraction by 4:

The ceiling with noisy labels. ERM agnostically PAC learns H\mathcal HH with

mH(ε,δ)≤256 dlog⁡(256/ε2)+64log⁡(4/δ)ε2.m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta) \le \frac{256 \, d \log(256/\varepsilon^2) + 64 \log(4/\delta)}{\varepsilon^2}.mH​(ε,δ)≤ε2256dlog(256/ε2)+64log(4/δ)​.

For the certificate’s noisy line, d=2d = 2d=2, ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1, δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05:

from math import log

def tangent(x, t):
    return log(t) + x / t - 1
xs = [k / 10 for k in range(1, 10_001)]
print(all(log(x) <= tangent(x, 7.0) + 1e-12 for x in xs))

def m_uc(eps, delta, d):
    return (64 * d * log(64 / eps**2)
            + 16 * log(4 / delta)) / eps**2
def m_agnostic(eps, delta, d):
    return m_uc(eps / 2, delta, d)
print(round(m_uc(0.1, 0.05, 2)), round(m_agnostic(0.1, 0.05, 2)))

It prints True (the log stays under its tangent at 10,000 test points) and 119191 547743. Those are the two numbers from the table in Step 3: 119,191 labels make every interval honest to within 0.1, and 547,743 make it honest to within 0.05, which is what ERM needs for estimation error 0.1. The certificate claimed 500.

### What this ceiling does and does not prove

Look at the shape: (dlog⁡(1/ε)+log⁡(1/δ))/ε2(d \log(1/\varepsilon) + \log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2(dlog(1/ε)+log(1/δ))/ε2, up to constants. The theorem of lesson 6a promises d+log⁡(1/δ)d + \log(1/\delta)d+log(1/δ) in the numerator, with no log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon)log(1/ε) next to the ddd. Our proof is off by that log factor. The log factor comes from Massart’s lemma, which measures the class at one scale. Removing it needs lesson 27’s chaining, which measures it at many scales at once, fed with a bound on the covering numbers of a class of VC dimension ddd that does not grow with mmm; that covering bound is a separate, harder proof that this course does not give. So be honest with the auditor: the ceiling we have proved is the theorem’s shape up to a factor of log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon)log(1/ε), with explicit constants, and its constants are large. Large, but proved.

The floor, part one: one message, two worlds

### A game you cannot win

Now switch sides. You are the adversary, and you want to embarrass every learner at once, using as few tools as possible. Here is the simplest weapon.

Pick one message, call it ccc, that the class can label either way: some hypothesis h+h^+h+ in H\mathcal HH calls it junk and some h−h^-h− calls it keep. (Any class with VC dimension at least 1 has such a message.) Now build two worlds. In both, every message that arrives is ccc. In the junk world, users label ccc junk 55% of the time and keep 45% of the time. In the keep world, it is the other way round. The best hypothesis in the junk world labels ccc junk and errs 45% of the time; labelling it keep errs 55% of the time. So whichever world you are in, guessing its direction wrong costs exactly 0.55−0.45=0.10.55 - 0.45 = 0.10.55−0.45=0.1 in true risk.

The learner sees mmm labels of the same message and must decide which world it is in. That is all it can do. With 10 labels, how often do you think the best possible learner guesses wrong? Write down a number before you read on.

The natural guess is the majority vote: say junk if more than half the labels say junk, flip a coin on a tie. Let’s simulate it, and compute its failure exactly with the binomial distribution: the number of labels that point the wrong way is a sum of mmm independent coins that each come up “wrong” with chance 0.45.

import random
from math import comb

def vote_loss(k, m):
    return 1 if 2 * k > m else 0.5 if 2 * k == m else 0
def exact_fail(m, eps):
    p = (1 - eps) / 2
    return sum(comb(m, k) * p**k * (1 - p)**(m - k)
               * vote_loss(k, m) for k in range(m + 1))
rng, eps, trials = random.Random(1), 0.1, 20_000
for m in (10, 80, 300):
    wrong = [sum(rng.random() < (1 - eps) / 2 for _ in range(m))
             for _ in range(trials)]
    sim = sum(vote_loss(k, m) for k in wrong) / trials
    print(m, round(sim, 3), round(exact_fail(m, eps), 3))

It prints

10 0.376 0.379
80 0.185 0.186
300 0.04 0.041

With 10 labels, the vote is wrong almost 38% of the time. With 80, still 19%. Only around 300 does it drop below 5%. Here k counts the labels pointing the wrong way, vote_loss is 1 when they win the vote and one half on a tie, and the simulation lands on the exact value each time.

Is the majority vote just a poor learner? No, and this is the heart of the floor: we will prove that no learner, however clever, can beat a certain bound in one of the two worlds. The lab lets you play the game first.

### The two worlds, formally

Let ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon \in (0, 1)ε∈(0,1). For b∈{0,1}b \in \{0, 1\}b∈{0,1}, the world Db\mathcal D_bDb​ puts all its probability on the two examples (c,b)(c, b)(c,b) and (c,1−b)(c, 1 - b)(c,1−b):

Db((c,b))=1+ε2,Db((c,1−b))=1−ε2.\mathcal D_b\big((c, b)\big) = \frac{1 + \varepsilon}{2}, \qquad \mathcal D_b\big((c, 1 - b)\big) = \frac{1 - \varepsilon}{2}.Db​((c,b))=21+ε​,Db​((c,1−b))=21−ε​.

Here Db(⋅)\mathcal D_b(\cdot)Db​(⋅) is the probability that world bbb gives to one example, (c,b)(c, b)(c,b) is “message ccc with label bbb”, and 1−b1 - b1−b is the other label. In plain words: in world bbb, message ccc carries label bbb a little more than half the time. With ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1, that is 0.550.550.55 and 0.450.450.45, the story above.

The true risk of any hypothesis hhh in world bbb depends only on its label at ccc: if h(c)=bh(c) = bh(c)=b, it errs exactly when the label is 1−b1 - b1−b, with chance (1−ε)/2(1 - \varepsilon)/2(1−ε)/2; otherwise it errs with chance (1+ε)/2(1 + \varepsilon)/2(1+ε)/2. Since h+h^+h+ and h−h^-h− are in H\mathcal HH, the best in the class is (1−ε)/2(1 - \varepsilon)/2(1−ε)/2, and so the estimation error of the learner’s output is

LDb(A(S))−min⁡h∈HLDb(h)=ε⋅1[A(S)(c)≠b].L_{\mathcal D_b}(A(S)) - \min_{h \in \mathcal H} L_{\mathcal D_b}(h) = \varepsilon \cdot \mathbb 1\big[A(S)(c) \neq b\big].LDb​​(A(S))−h∈Hmin​LDb​​(h)=ε⋅1[A(S)(c)=b].

A(S)(c)A(S)(c)A(S)(c) is the label the learner’s hypothesis gives to ccc, and the indicator is 1 when that label is not the world’s direction. In plain words: the learner pays ε\varepsilonε if it guesses the world wrong, and nothing if it guesses right.

Every training sequence from either world is mmm copies of ccc with labels y=(y1,…,ym)∈{0,1}my = (y_1, \dots, y_m) \in \{0, 1\}^my=(y1​,…,ym​)∈{0,1}m, so a learner is, for our purposes, just a guessing rule ggg that maps a label vector yyy to a guess g(y)∈{0,1}g(y) \in \{0, 1\}g(y)∈{0,1}. (A learner that also flips its own coins is a mixture of such rules; every bound below holds for each rule, hence for the mixture.) Write Pb(y)P_b(y)Pb​(y) for the chance of seeing yyy in world bbb: each label equal to bbb contributes a factor (1+ε)/2(1 + \varepsilon)/2(1+ε)/2, each other label a factor (1−ε)/2(1 - \varepsilon)/2(1−ε)/2, and independence multiplies them.

### Step 1: one world must hurt

We cannot know which world the learner will face, but the adversary can choose the worse one, and the worse of two numbers is at least their average:

max⁡b∈{0,1}Pb[g(y)≠b]≥12(P1[g(y)=0]+P0[g(y)=1])=12∑y(P1(y) 1[g(y)=0]+P0(y) 1[g(y)=1])≥12∑ymin⁡(P1(y),P0(y)).\max_{b \in \{0,1\}} P_b[g(y) \neq b] \ge \frac12 \Big( P_1[g(y) = 0] + P_0[g(y) = 1] \Big) = \frac12 \sum_{y} \Big( P_1(y) \, \mathbb 1[g(y) = 0] + P_0(y) \, \mathbb 1[g(y) = 1] \Big) \ge \frac12 \sum_y \min\big(P_1(y), P_0(y)\big).b∈{0,1}max​Pb​[g(y)=b]≥21​(P1​[g(y)=0]+P0​[g(y)=1])=21​y∑​(P1​(y)1[g(y)=0]+P0​(y)1[g(y)=1])≥21​y∑​min(P1​(y),P0​(y)).

From left to right: Pb[g(y)≠b]P_b[g(y) \neq b]Pb​[g(y)=b] is the chance that rule ggg guesses wrong in world bbb, and max⁡b\max_bmaxb​ takes the worse world. The first inequality replaces the maximum by the average. The equality writes each probability as a sum over all 2m2^m2m label vectors yyy, keeping those on which ggg guesses wrong. The last step is the key: for each yyy, exactly one of the two indicators is 1, so the bracket is either P1(y)P_1(y)P1​(y) or P0(y)P_0(y)P0​(y), and either way it is at least the smaller of the two, min⁡(P1(y),P0(y))\min(P_1(y), P_0(y))min(P1​(y),P0​(y)). In plain words: whatever the rule does with a label vector, it is wrong in one of the worlds, and the overlap of the two worlds’ distributions is a toll no rule can dodge. And the majority vote pays exactly this toll, because it always picks the world under which yyy is more likely, which is the world with the larger of the two probabilities.

### Step 2: the overlap lemma

So we need a lower bound on the overlap ∑ymin⁡(P1(y),P0(y))\sum_y \min(P_1(y), P_0(y))∑y​min(P1​(y),P0​(y)). The tool is a quantity called the Bhattacharyya coefficient, B=∑yP1(y)P0(y)B = \sum_y \sqrt{P_1(y) P_0(y)}B=∑y​P1​(y)P0​(y)​: add up the geometric means of the two probabilities. It is 1 when the distributions are identical and 0 when they never overlap.

The overlap lemma. For any two probability distributions P,QP, QP,Q on a finite set, with B=∑yP(y)Q(y)B = \sum_y \sqrt{P(y)Q(y)}B=∑y​P(y)Q(y)​,

∑ymin⁡(P(y),Q(y))≥1−1−B2.\sum_y \min\big(P(y), Q(y)\big) \ge 1 - \sqrt{1 - B^2}.y∑​min(P(y),Q(y))≥1−1−B2​.

On the left, the shared mass of the two distributions; on the right, a function of BBB that is 0 when B=0B = 0B=0 and 1 when B=1B = 1B=1. In plain words: two distributions that are similar in the square-root sense must share a lot of mass. With B=0.951B = 0.951B=0.951, the right side is 1−1−0.904≈0.691 - \sqrt{1 - 0.904} \approx 0.691−1−0.904​≈0.69.

First, for two numbers, min⁡(p,q)=12(p+q−∣p−q∣)\min(p, q) = \frac12(p + q - |p - q|)min(p,q)=21​(p+q−∣p−q∣): the average minus half the gap. Summing over yyy, and using that each distribution sums to 1, ∑ymin⁡(P,Q)=1−12∑y∣P(y)−Q(y)∣\sum_y \min(P, Q) = 1 - \frac12 \sum_y |P(y) - Q(y)|∑y​min(P,Q)=1−21​∑y​∣P(y)−Q(y)∣.

Second, factor each gap as a difference of squares: ∣p−q∣=∣p−q∣ (p+q)|p - q| = |\sqrt p - \sqrt q| \, (\sqrt p + \sqrt q)∣p−q∣=∣p​−q​∣(p​+q​). Then apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, which says that for any two lists of numbers, ∑yuyvy≤∑yuy2 ∑yvy2\sum_y u_y v_y \le \sqrt{\sum_y u_y^2} \, \sqrt{\sum_y v_y^2}∑y​uy​vy​≤∑y​uy2​​∑y​vy2​​:

∑y∣P(y)−Q(y)∣≤∑y(P(y)−Q(y))2 ∑y(P(y)+Q(y))2.\sum_y |P(y) - Q(y)| \le \sqrt{\sum_y \big(\sqrt{P(y)} - \sqrt{Q(y)}\big)^2} \, \sqrt{\sum_y \big(\sqrt{P(y)} + \sqrt{Q(y)}\big)^2}.y∑​∣P(y)−Q(y)∣≤y∑​(P(y)​−Q(y)​)2​y∑​(P(y)​+Q(y)​)2​.

Third, expand the squares. (p−q)2=p+q−2pq(\sqrt p - \sqrt q)^2 = p + q - 2\sqrt{pq}(p​−q​)2=p+q−2pq​, which sums to 2−2B2 - 2B2−2B; likewise (p+q)2(\sqrt p + \sqrt q)^2(p​+q​)2 sums to 2+2B2 + 2B2+2B. So ∑y∣P−Q∣≤(2−2B)(2+2B)=21−B2\sum_y |P - Q| \le \sqrt{(2 - 2B)(2 + 2B)} = 2\sqrt{1 - B^2}∑y​∣P−Q∣≤(2−2B)(2+2B)​=21−B2​, and putting this into the first step gives ∑ymin⁡(P,Q)≥1−1−B2\sum_y \min(P, Q) \ge 1 - \sqrt{1 - B^2}∑y​min(P,Q)≥1−1−B2​. ■\blacksquare■

For our two worlds, the coefficient is easy to compute, because a sum over all label vectors of a product over labels factors into a product of sums over single labels:

B=∏i=1m(1+ε2⋅1−ε2+1−ε2⋅1+ε2)=(1−ε2)m=(1−ε2)m/2.B = \prod_{i=1}^{m} \left( \sqrt{\tfrac{1 + \varepsilon}{2} \cdot \tfrac{1 - \varepsilon}{2}} + \sqrt{\tfrac{1 - \varepsilon}{2} \cdot \tfrac{1 + \varepsilon}{2}} \right) = \left( \sqrt{1 - \varepsilon^2} \right)^m = (1 - \varepsilon^2)^{m/2}.B=i=1∏m​(21+ε​⋅21−ε​​+21−ε​⋅21+ε​​)=(1−ε2​)m=(1−ε2)m/2.

The ∏\prod∏ is a product over the mmm labels; for one label, whichever value it takes, the two worlds give it probabilities (1+ε)/2(1+\varepsilon)/2(1+ε)/2 and (1−ε)/2(1-\varepsilon)/2(1−ε)/2 in some order, so each label contributes twice the geometric mean of the two, 1−ε2\sqrt{1 - \varepsilon^2}1−ε2​. In plain words: each extra label pulls the two worlds apart by a factor of 1−ε2\sqrt{1 - \varepsilon^2}1−ε2​. With ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1 and m=10m = 10m=10, B=0.995≈0.951B = 0.99^5 \approx 0.951B=0.995≈0.951.

Putting Steps 1 and 2 together: every rule, in one of the two worlds, guesses wrong with probability at least

12(1−1−(1−ε2)m).\frac12 \left( 1 - \sqrt{1 - (1 - \varepsilon^2)^m} \right).21​(1−1−(1−ε2)m​).

Let’s check the lemma against the exact numbers, grouping label vectors by how many 1s they contain (all (mk)\binom{m}{k}(km​) vectors with kkk ones have the same probability):

from math import comb, sqrt

def overlap(m, eps):
    hi, lo = (1 + eps) / 2, (1 - eps) / 2
    sum_min = bc = 0.0
    for k in range(m + 1):
        p1 = hi**k * lo**(m - k)
        p0 = lo**k * hi**(m - k)
        sum_min += comb(m, k) * min(p1, p0)
        bc += comb(m, k) * sqrt(p1 * p0)
    return sum_min, bc
for m in (10, 80):
    sum_min, bc = overlap(m, 0.1)
    print(m, round(sum_min / 2, 4), round(bc, 4),
          round((1 - 0.1**2) ** (m / 2), 4),
          round((1 - sqrt(1 - bc**2)) / 2, 4))

It prints 10 0.3786 0.951 0.951 0.3454 and 80 0.1857 0.669 0.669 0.1284. The first column after mmm is half the overlap: 0.3786 and 0.1857, the majority vote’s exact failure rates from the simulation. So the majority vote pays exactly the toll. The next two columns agree: the coefficient computed by brute force equals (1−ε2)m/2(1 - \varepsilon^2)^{m/2}(1−ε2)m/2. The last column is the lemma’s floor, 0.345 and 0.128, safely below.

### Step 3: from a power to an exponential

The floor (1−ε2)m(1 - \varepsilon^2)^m(1−ε2)m is exact but awkward. We trade it for an exponential using one inequality: for 0≤x≤120 \le x \le \frac120≤x≤21​,

log⁡(1−x)≥−x1−x≥−2x.\log(1 - x) \ge -\frac{x}{1 - x} \ge -2x.log(1−x)≥−1−xx​≥−2x.

The first step holds because log⁡11−x=log⁡(1+x1−x)≤x1−x\log \frac{1}{1 - x} = \log\left(1 + \frac{x}{1 - x}\right) \le \frac{x}{1 - x}log1−x1​=log(1+1−xx​)≤1−xx​, using log⁡(1+u)≤u\log(1 + u) \le ulog(1+u)≤u, which is the tangent-line lemma at t=1t = 1t=1. The second holds because 1−x≥121 - x \ge \frac121−x≥21​. So if ε2≤12\varepsilon^2 \le \frac12ε2≤21​, then (1−ε2)m≥e−2mε2(1 - \varepsilon^2)^m \ge e^{-2m\varepsilon^2}(1−ε2)m≥e−2mε2. The function u↦12(1−1−u)u \mapsto \frac12(1 - \sqrt{1 - u})u↦21​(1−1−u​) grows with uuu, so every rule fails in one world with probability at least

12(1−1−e−2mε2).\frac12 \left( 1 - \sqrt{1 - e^{-2m\varepsilon^2}} \right).21​(1−1−e−2mε2​).

In plain words: the best possible failure rate shrinks with mε2m\varepsilon^2mε2, not faster. That product mε2m\varepsilon^2mε2 is the whole story of the 1/ε21/\varepsilon^21/ε2 rate: to keep the failure fixed while halving ε\varepsilonε, you must quadruple mmm.

### The floor theorem, part one

The floor with noisy labels, confidence part. Let H\mathcal HH have VC dimension at least 1, let 0<ε<1/20 < \varepsilon < 1/\sqrt20<ε<1/2​ and 0<δ<1/40 < \delta < 1/40<δ<1/4. If

m<log⁡(1/(4δ))2ε2,m < \frac{\log\big(1/(4\delta)\big)}{2\varepsilon^2},m<2ε2log(1/(4δ))​,

then for every learner there is a distribution on which it misses with probability greater than δ\deltaδ. Hence mH(ε,δ)≥log⁡(1/(4δ))/(2ε2)m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta) \ge \log(1/(4\delta))/(2\varepsilon^2)mH​(ε,δ)≥log(1/(4δ))/(2ε2).

The numerator is the log of 1/(4δ)1/(4\delta)1/(4δ), positive because δ<1/4\delta < 1/4δ<1/4; the denominator is twice ε2\varepsilon^2ε2. In plain words: fewer than about half of log⁡(1/(4δ))/ε2\log(1/(4\delta))/\varepsilon^2log(1/(4δ))/ε2 labels cannot buy accuracy ε\varepsilonε with confidence 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, for any learner. For the certificate, log⁡5/0.02≈80.5\log 5 / 0.02 \approx 80.5log5/0.02≈80.5.

Proof. One subtlety first. A miss means estimation error greater than ε\varepsilonε, but our two worlds charge exactly ε\varepsilonε for a wrong guess, which is not a miss. So we build the worlds with a slightly larger gap. The right side of the condition shrinks continuously as ε\varepsilonε grows, and it is strictly greater than mmm at ε\varepsilonε itself, so we can pick ε′\varepsilon'ε′ with ε<ε′<1/2\varepsilon < \varepsilon' < 1/\sqrt2ε<ε′<1/2​ and still m<log⁡(1/(4δ))/(2ε′2)m < \log(1/(4\delta))/(2\varepsilon'^2)m<log(1/(4δ))/(2ε′2).

Build the two worlds with ε′\varepsilon'ε′ in place of ε\varepsilonε. A wrong guess now costs ε′>ε\varepsilon' > \varepsilonε′>ε, a genuine miss. Since ε′2<12\varepsilon'^2 < \frac12ε′2<21​, Step 3 applies: in one of the worlds the learner guesses wrong with probability at least 12(1−1−e−2mε′2)\frac12(1 - \sqrt{1 - e^{-2m\varepsilon'^2}})21​(1−1−e−2mε′2​).

The condition on mmm says 2mε′2<log⁡(1/(4δ))2m\varepsilon'^2 < \log(1/(4\delta))2mε′2<log(1/(4δ)), so e−2mε′2>4δe^{-2m\varepsilon'^2} > 4\deltae−2mε′2>4δ, so 1−e−2mε′2<1−4δ1 - e^{-2m\varepsilon'^2} < 1 - 4\delta1−e−2mε′2<1−4δ, and the failure probability is strictly greater than 12(1−1−4δ)\frac12(1 - \sqrt{1 - 4\delta})21​(1−1−4δ​).

Finally, 12(1−1−4δ)≥δ\frac12(1 - \sqrt{1 - 4\delta}) \ge \delta21​(1−1−4δ​)≥δ. Rearranged, that is 1−4δ≤1−2δ\sqrt{1 - 4\delta} \le 1 - 2\delta1−4δ​≤1−2δ; both sides are nonnegative since δ<1/4\delta < 1/4δ<1/4, so we may square: 1−4δ≤1−4δ+4δ21 - 4\delta \le 1 - 4\delta + 4\delta^21−4δ≤1−4δ+4δ2, which is true. So the learner misses with probability greater than δ\deltaδ. ■\blacksquare■

from math import exp, log, sqrt

xs = [k / 1000 for k in range(0, 501)]
print(all(log(1 - x) >= -2 * x for x in xs))
deltas = [k / 1000 for k in range(1, 250)]
print(all((1 - sqrt(1 - 4 * dl)) / 2 >= dl for dl in deltas))
eps, delta = 0.1, 0.05
print(round(log(1 / (4 * delta)) / (2 * eps**2), 2))
m = 80
floor_bound = (1 - sqrt(1 - exp(-2 * m * eps**2))) / 2
print(round(floor_bound, 4), floor_bound > delta)

It prints True, True, 80.47, then 0.0533 True. The two inequalities hold on a fine grid, the floor for the certificate is 80.47 labels, and at 80 labels the proved failure rate, 0.0533, is just above δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05. The exact failure of the best learner at 80 labels is 0.186, far above. The proof gives away a lot, but not so much that the floor becomes useless.

The floor, part two: ddd messages, ddd coins

### Spreading the labels thin

The first floor used one message, so it could only charge for confidence: it explains the log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ) but says nothing about ddd. To make the VC dimension appear, the adversary uses all of it.

Take ddd messages that the class shatters. For each of them, flip a hidden coin to decide its direction, junk or keep, and let users label it in that direction a little more than half the time, with bias ρ\rhoρ (the Greek letter rho): in its direction with chance (1+ρ)/2(1 + \rho)/2(1+ρ)/2. Messages arrive uniformly at random. The learner’s mmm labels are now spread over ddd messages, about m/dm/dm/d each, and it must guess every message’s direction. Each wrong guess costs ρ/d\rho/dρ/d in true risk.

Picture ten balance beams, one per message, with labels dropping onto them at random, each label tipping its beam a little toward junk or toward keep. With 30 labels, each beam gets about three. How many beams would you expect to tip the wrong way?

[diagram:d-coins: built on the lesson page]

import random
from math import sqrt

d, rho, trials = 10, 0.2, 4_000
rng = random.Random(2)
def wrong_fraction(m):
    b = [rng.randint(0, 1) for _ in range(d)]
    votes = [0] * d
    for _ in range(m):
        i = rng.randrange(d)
        y = b[i] if rng.random() < (1 + rho) / 2 else 1 - b[i]
        votes[i] += 1 if y == 1 else -1
    guess = [int(v > 0) if v else rng.randint(0, 1)
             for v in votes]
    return sum(g != t for g, t in zip(guess, b)) / d
for m in (10, 30, 100):
    sim = sum(wrong_fraction(m) for _ in range(trials)) / trials
    bound = (1 - sqrt(2 * rho**2 * m / d)) / 2
    print(m, round(sim, 3), round(bound, 3))

It prints

10 0.433 0.359
30 0.368 0.255
100 0.265 0.053

The middle column is the fraction of beams the majority vote gets wrong, averaged over 4,000 games; a beam with no labels, or a tie, gets a coin flip. With 30 labels, more than a third of the beams are still wrong. The last column is the floor we are about to prove, 12(1−2ρ2m/d)\frac12(1 - \sqrt{2\rho^2 m/d})21​(1−2ρ2m/d​): always below the simulation, and above one quarter as long as mmm is below d/(8ρ2)=31.25d/(8\rho^2) = 31.25d/(8ρ2)=31.25. Hold on to that threshold.

### The ddd worlds, formally

Let C={c1,…,cd}C = \{c_1, \dots, c_d\}C={c1​,…,cd​} be shattered by H\mathcal HH, and let 0<ρ≤1/20 < \rho \le 1/\sqrt20<ρ≤1/2​. For each direction vector b=(b1,…,bd)∈{0,1}db = (b_1, \dots, b_d) \in \{0, 1\}^db=(b1​,…,bd​)∈{0,1}d, the world Db\mathcal D_bDb​ is

Db((ci,bi))=1d⋅1+ρ2,Db((ci,1−bi))=1d⋅1−ρ2,i∈[d].\mathcal D_b\big((c_i, b_i)\big) = \frac1d \cdot \frac{1 + \rho}{2}, \qquad \mathcal D_b\big((c_i, 1 - b_i)\big) = \frac1d \cdot \frac{1 - \rho}{2}, \qquad i \in [d].Db​((ci​,bi​))=d1​⋅21+ρ​,Db​((ci​,1−bi​))=d1​⋅21−ρ​,i∈[d].

Here [d]={1,…,d}[d] = \{1, \dots, d\}[d]={1,…,d}, the 1d\frac1dd1​ is the chance that message cic_ici​ is the one that arrives, and the second factor is the chance of each label given that it arrived. In plain words: pick one of the ddd messages uniformly, then label it in its direction with chance (1+ρ)/2(1+\rho)/2(1+ρ)/2. With d=3d = 3d=3 and ρ=0.2\rho = 0.2ρ=0.2, example (c1,b1)(c_1, b_1)(c1​,b1​) has probability 13⋅0.6=0.2\frac13 \cdot 0.6 = 0.231​⋅0.6=0.2.

The risk identity. For every function f:X→{0,1}f: \mathcal X \to \{0,1\}f:X→{0,1},

LDb(f)−min⁡h∈HLDb(h)=ρ⋅∣{i∈[d]:f(ci)≠bi}∣d.L_{\mathcal D_b}(f) - \min_{h \in \mathcal H} L_{\mathcal D_b}(h) = \rho \cdot \frac{\left| \{ i \in [d] : f(c_i) \neq b_i \} \right|}{d}.LDb​​(f)−h∈Hmin​LDb​​(h)=ρ⋅d∣{i∈[d]:f(ci​)=bi​}∣​.

The set in the numerator collects the messages on which fff goes against the world’s direction, the colon reading “such that”, and the bars count them. In plain words: the estimation error is ρ\rhoρ times the fraction of messages fff gets backwards.

Proof. Message cic_ici​ arrives with chance 1d\frac1dd1​. If f(ci)=bif(c_i) = b_if(ci​)=bi​, fff errs on it with chance (1−ρ)/2(1 - \rho)/2(1−ρ)/2; otherwise with chance (1+ρ)/2(1 + \rho)/2(1+ρ)/2. So LDb(f)L_{\mathcal D_b}(f)LDb​​(f) is 1d\frac1dd1​ times the sum of these over iii. No function can do better than (1−ρ)/2(1-\rho)/2(1−ρ)/2 on any message, and because CCC is shattered, some h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H has h(ci)=bih(c_i) = b_ih(ci​)=bi​ for every iii and achieves (1−ρ)/2(1 - \rho)/2(1−ρ)/2 on all of them. So the best in the class is (1−ρ)/2(1 - \rho)/2(1−ρ)/2, and each backwards message adds 1d(1+ρ2−1−ρ2)=ρd\frac1d\left(\frac{1+\rho}{2} - \frac{1-\rho}{2}\right) = \frac{\rho}{d}d1​(21+ρ​−21−ρ​)=dρ​. ■\blacksquare■

d, rho = 3, 0.2
b, f = (1, 0, 1), (1, 1, 0)

def risk(g):
    total = 0.0
    for i in range(d):
        for y in (0, 1):
            p_y = (1 + rho) / 2 if y == b[i] else (1 - rho) / 2
            total += p_y / d * (g[i] != y)
    return total
mismatches = sum(f_i != b_i for f_i, b_i in zip(f, b))
print(round(risk(b), 4), round(risk(f), 4))
print(round(risk(f) - risk(b), 4), round(rho * mismatches / d, 4))

It prints 0.4 0.5333 and 0.1333 0.1333: the best hypothesis errs 40% of the time, which is (1−0.2)/2(1 - 0.2)/2(1−0.2)/2; fff gets two of the three messages backwards and errs 53.3%; the difference matches 0.2⋅2/30.2 \cdot 2/30.2⋅2/3.

### Step 1: average over the worlds

Here is lesson 5’s trick. The adversary may pick the worst world, and the worst is at least the average. Choose bbb uniformly at random from all 2d2^d2d direction vectors; then

max⁡bES∼Dbm[LDb(A(S))−min⁡h∈HLDb(h)]≥Eb ES∼Dbm[ρd∑i=1d1[A(S)(ci)≠bi]]=ρd∑i=1dEb ES 1[A(S)(ci)≠bi].\max_{b} \mathbb E_{S \sim \mathcal D_b^m}\left[ L_{\mathcal D_b}(A(S)) - \min_{h \in \mathcal H} L_{\mathcal D_b}(h) \right] \ge \mathbb E_{b} \, \mathbb E_{S \sim \mathcal D_b^m} \left[ \frac{\rho}{d} \sum_{i=1}^{d} \mathbb 1\big[A(S)(c_i) \neq b_i\big] \right] = \frac{\rho}{d} \sum_{i=1}^{d} \mathbb E_{b} \, \mathbb E_{S} \, \mathbb 1\big[A(S)(c_i) \neq b_i\big].bmax​ES∼Dbm​​[LDb​​(A(S))−h∈Hmin​LDb​​(h)]≥Eb​ES∼Dbm​​[dρ​i=1∑d​1[A(S)(ci​)=bi​]]=dρ​i=1∑d​Eb​ES​1[A(S)(ci​)=bi​].

On the left, the expected estimation error in the worst world; ES∼Dbm\mathbb E_{S \sim \mathcal D_b^m}ES∼Dbm​​ averages over the training sequences of that world. In the middle, the risk identity has replaced the estimation error by ρ/d\rho/dρ/d times the number of backwards messages, and Eb\mathbb E_bEb​ averages over the uniformly random world. On the right, linearity of expectation (the average of a sum is the sum of the averages) splits the count into one term per message. In plain words: the worst world costs at least the average world, and the average world’s cost is ρ/d\rho/dρ/d times the expected number of messages guessed backwards.

To sample SSS from Db\mathcal D_bDb​, first choose which message each example is, j=(j1,…,jm)j = (j_1, \dots, j_m)j=(j1​,…,jm​) with each jrj_rjr​ uniform on [d][d][d], then draw each label yry_ryr​ toward bjrb_{j_r}bjr​​ with chance (1+ρ)/2(1 + \rho)/2(1+ρ)/2. The positions jjj do not depend on bbb.

### Step 2: one message at a time, and the majority vote is best

Fix the positions jjj and one message iii. Let nin_ini​ be how many of the mmm examples landed on cic_ici​, let yIy^IyI be their labels, and let y¬Iy^{\neg I}y¬I be all the other labels. Now an important observation: the labels yIy^IyI depend only on bib_ibi​, and the other labels depend only on the other directions b¬ib_{\neg i}b¬i​. Since bbb is uniform, its coordinates are independent fair coins, so the pair (bi,yI)(b_i, y^I)(bi​,yI) is independent of y¬Iy^{\neg I}y¬I. The other messages’ labels tell the learner nothing about bib_ibi​.

So, for each fixed value of the other labels, the learner faces exactly the two-world game of part one with nin_ini​ labels and gap ρ\rhoρ: the direction bib_ibi​ is a fair coin, the labels yIy^IyI lean toward it, and the learner’s answer at cic_ici​ is some guess. Step 1 of part one says the chance of a wrong guess, averaged over bib_ibi​, is at least half the overlap, and the overlap does not depend on the other labels. Averaging over them changes nothing, so

Eb Ey 1[A(S)(ci)≠bi]≥12∑yImin⁡(P(yI∣bi=1),P(yI∣bi=0))≥12(1−1−e−2ρ2ni).\mathbb E_{b} \, \mathbb E_{y} \, \mathbb 1\big[A(S)(c_i) \neq b_i\big] \ge \frac12 \sum_{y^I} \min\big(P(y^I \mid b_i = 1), P(y^I \mid b_i = 0)\big) \ge \frac12\left(1 - \sqrt{1 - e^{-2\rho^2 n_i}}\right).Eb​Ey​1[A(S)(ci​)=bi​]≥21​yI∑​min(P(yI∣bi​=1),P(yI∣bi​=0))≥21​(1−1−e−2ρ2ni​​).

P(yI∣bi=1)P(y^I \mid b_i = 1)P(yI∣bi​=1) is the chance of the labels yIy^IyI when message iii leans junk; the vertical bar reads “given”. The second inequality is the overlap lemma and the exponential step of part one, with nin_ini​ labels and ρ\rhoρ in place of ε\varepsilonε (allowed because ρ2≤12\rho^2 \le \frac12ρ2≤21​). When ni=0n_i = 0ni​=0, both sides are 12\frac1221​: with no labels, you can only flip a coin.

The first inequality becomes an equality for one learner: the majority vote, which at each message guesses the direction that most of its labels point to, with a coin flip on a tie. As we saw, it picks the larger of the two probabilities for every yIy^IyI, so it pays exactly the overlap. This rule is also called the maximum-likelihood learner, because it picks the direction under which the observed labels are most likely. In plain words: on every message, the best any learner can do, on average over the worlds, is the majority vote, and even the majority vote errs at least this often. You can check the “best” part by brute force: with three labels there are 23=82^3 = 823=8 label vectors and 28=2562^8 = 25628=256 deterministic guessing rules.

from itertools import product

n, rho = 3, 0.2
ys = list(product([0, 1], repeat=n))
def p(y, b):
    hits = sum(t == b for t in y)
    return ((1 + rho) / 2)**hits * ((1 - rho) / 2)**(n - hits)
def error(g):
    return sum(0.5 * p(y, b) * (g[k] != b)
               for k, y in enumerate(ys) for b in (0, 1))
rules = list(product([0, 1], repeat=len(ys)))
best = min(error(g) for g in rules)
majority = tuple(int(2 * sum(y) > n) for y in ys)
print(len(rules), round(best, 4), round(error(majority), 4))

It prints 256 0.352 0.352: of all 256 rules, the best errs 35.2% of the time, and the majority vote is that best.

### Step 3: from nin_ini​ to m/dm/dm/d

The bound depends on nin_ini​, which is random. Two small inequalities make it depend on mmm instead.

First, 1−e−a≤a1 - e^{-a} \le a1−e−a≤a for a≥0a \ge 0a≥0 (the exponential lies above its tangent line 1−a1 - a1−a). With a=2ρ2nia = 2\rho^2 n_ia=2ρ2ni​, 1−e−2ρ2ni≤2ρ2ni\sqrt{1 - e^{-2\rho^2 n_i}} \le \sqrt{2\rho^2 n_i}1−e−2ρ2ni​​≤2ρ2ni​​, so the per-message bound is at least 12(1−2ρ2ni)\frac12(1 - \sqrt{2\rho^2 n_i})21​(1−2ρ2ni​​).

Second, for any nonnegative random quantity XXX, E[X]≤E[X]\mathbb E[\sqrt X] \le \sqrt{\mathbb E[X]}E[X​]≤E[X]​. This is a case of Jensen’s inequality for the concave square root, and here is a one-line proof: the variance of X\sqrt XX​ is never negative, so (EX)2≤E[(X)2]=E[X](\mathbb E \sqrt X)^2 \le \mathbb E[(\sqrt X)^2] = \mathbb E[X](EX​)2≤E[(X​)2]=E[X].

Each of the mmm examples lands on cic_ici​ with chance 1d\frac1dd1​, so Ej[ni]=m/d\mathbb E_j[n_i] = m/dEj​[ni​]=m/d. Averaging the per-message bound over the positions jjj:

Ej[12(1−2ρ2ni)]=12(1−2ρ2 Ej[ni])≥12(1−2ρ2md).\mathbb E_j \left[ \frac12\left(1 - \sqrt{2\rho^2 n_i}\right) \right] = \frac12 \left( 1 - \sqrt{2\rho^2} \, \mathbb E_j\big[\sqrt{n_i}\big] \right) \ge \frac12\left(1 - \sqrt{\frac{2\rho^2 m}{d}}\right).Ej​[21​(1−2ρ2ni​​)]=21​(1−2ρ2​Ej​[ni​​])≥21​(1−d2ρ2m​​).

The equality pulls the constants out of the average; the inequality is Jensen with Ej[ni]=m/d\mathbb E_j[n_i] = m/dEj​[ni​]=m/d. For the beams, d=10d = 10d=10 and m=30m = 30m=30, so nin_ini​ counts how many of 30 coins with chance 1/101/101/10 come up, and its exact distribution gives Ej[ni]\mathbb E_j[\sqrt{n_i}]Ej​[ni​​]:

from math import comb, sqrt

d, m = 10, 30
p = 1 / d
mean_root = sum(comb(m, n) * p**n * (1 - p)**(m - n) * sqrt(n)
                for n in range(m + 1))
print(round(mean_root, 4), round(sqrt(m / d), 4))

It prints 1.6413 1.7321: the average of ni\sqrt{n_i}ni​​ sits below 3\sqrt{3}3​, as Jensen promises.

Now sum over the ddd messages in Step 1’s right-hand side: ρd\frac{\rho}{d}dρ​ times ddd copies of the same bound.

max⁡bES∼Dbm[LDb(A(S))−min⁡h∈HLDb(h)]≥ρ2(1−2ρ2md).\max_{b} \mathbb E_{S \sim \mathcal D_b^m}\left[ L_{\mathcal D_b}(A(S)) - \min_{h \in \mathcal H} L_{\mathcal D_b}(h) \right] \ge \frac{\rho}{2} \left( 1 - \sqrt{\frac{2\rho^2 m}{d}} \right).bmax​ES∼Dbm​​[LDb​​(A(S))−h∈Hmin​LDb​​(h)]≥2ρ​(1−d2ρ2m​​).

In plain words: in the worst of the ddd-coin worlds, every learner’s expected estimation error is at least ρ/2\rho/2ρ/2 times one minus the square root of 2ρ2m/d2\rho^2 m/d2ρ2m/d. The key quantity is ρ2m/d\rho^2 m / dρ2m/d: labels per message times the squared bias. If m<d/(8ρ2)m < d/(8\rho^2)m<d/(8ρ2), then 2ρ2m/d<142\rho^2 m/d < \frac142ρ2m/d<41​, the square root is below 12\frac1221​, and the expected estimation error exceeds ρ/4\rho/4ρ/4. ### Step 4: from an average to a probability

An expected estimation error above ρ/4\rho/4ρ/4 does not yet mean frequent misses: maybe the error is huge rarely and tiny usually. But it cannot be huge, because it is at most ρ\rhoρ (all messages backwards). A quantity trapped in a range with a high average must often be high. Here is the precise version, the same reasoning as lesson 5’s 1/71/71/7.

A bounded-average lemma. If ZZZ takes values in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] and 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1, then P[Z>a]≥E[Z]−a1−a\mathbb P[Z > a] \ge \dfrac{\mathbb E[Z] - a}{1 - a}P[Z>a]≥1−aE[Z]−a​.

Proof. Let q=P[Z>a]q = \mathbb P[Z > a]q=P[Z>a]. When Z≤aZ \le aZ≤a it contributes at most aaa to the average; when Z>aZ > aZ>a it contributes at most 1. So E[Z]≤a(1−q)+q\mathbb E[Z] \le a(1 - q) + qE[Z]≤a(1−q)+q, which rearranges to q≥(E[Z]−a)/(1−a)q \ge (\mathbb E[Z] - a)/(1 - a)q≥(E[Z]−a)/(1−a). ■\blacksquare■

Apply it to Z=Z =Z= estimation error divided by ρ\rhoρ, which lies in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] by the risk identity, in the worst world, with E[Z]>14\mathbb E[Z] > \frac14E[Z]>41​. Choose ρ=8ε\rho = 8\varepsilonρ=8ε and a=ε/ρ=18a = \varepsilon/\rho = \frac18a=ε/ρ=81​:

P[LDb(A(S))−min⁡hLDb(h)>ε]=P[Z>18]>14−181−18=17.\mathbb P\left[ L_{\mathcal D_b}(A(S)) - \min_{h} L_{\mathcal D_b}(h) > \varepsilon \right] = \mathbb P\left[ Z > \tfrac18 \right] > \frac{\frac14 - \frac18}{1 - \frac18} = \frac17.P[LDb​​(A(S))−hmin​LDb​​(h)>ε]=P[Z>81​]>1−81​41​−81​​=71​.

The condition ρ≤1/2\rho \le 1/\sqrt2ρ≤1/2​ becomes ε≤1/(82)≈0.088\varepsilon \le 1/(8\sqrt2) \approx 0.088ε≤1/(82​)≈0.088, and m<d/(8ρ2)m < d/(8\rho^2)m<d/(8ρ2) becomes m<d/(512ε2)m < d/(512\varepsilon^2)m<d/(512ε2).

The floor with noisy labels, dimension part. Let H\mathcal HH have VC dimension d≥1d \ge 1d≥1, let 0<ε≤1/(82)0 < \varepsilon \le 1/(8\sqrt2)0<ε≤1/(82​) and 0<δ<1/70 < \delta < 1/70<δ<1/7. If m<d/(512ε2)m < d/(512\varepsilon^2)m<d/(512ε2), every learner misses with probability greater than 1/7>δ1/7 > \delta1/7>δ on some distribution. Hence mH(ε,δ)≥d/(512ε2)m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta) \ge d/(512\varepsilon^2)mH​(ε,δ)≥d/(512ε2).

In plain words: fewer than d/(512ε2)d/(512\varepsilon^2)d/(512ε2) labels leave some world where every learner misses more than one time in seven. The constant 512 is ugly, and the honest truth is that this proof spends constants freely; the shape d/ε2d/\varepsilon^2d/ε2 is what matters.

### Both floors together

For δ≤1/8\delta \le 1/8δ≤1/8, both parts apply, so mH(ε,δ)m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta)mH​(ε,δ) is at least the larger of the two floors, and the larger of two numbers is at least their average. Also, δ≤1/8\delta \le 1/8δ≤1/8 gives log⁡(1/δ)≥3log⁡2\log(1/\delta) \ge 3\log 2log(1/δ)≥3log2, so log⁡4=2log⁡2≤23log⁡(1/δ)\log 4 = 2\log 2 \le \frac23 \log(1/\delta)log4=2log2≤32​log(1/δ) and log⁡(1/(4δ))≥13log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/(4\delta)) \ge \frac13 \log(1/\delta)log(1/(4δ))≥31​log(1/δ). Then

mH(ε,δ)≥12(log⁡(1/δ)6ε2+d512ε2)≥d+log⁡(1/δ)1024 ε2.m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta) \ge \frac12 \left( \frac{\log(1/\delta)}{6\varepsilon^2} + \frac{d}{512\varepsilon^2} \right) \ge \frac{d + \log(1/\delta)}{1024\,\varepsilon^2}.mH​(ε,δ)≥21​(6ε2log(1/δ)​+512ε2d​)≥1024ε2d+log(1/δ)​.

In plain words: for small enough ε\varepsilonε and δ\deltaδ, no learner can do with fewer than (d+log⁡(1/δ))/(1024ε2)(d + \log(1/\delta))/(1024\varepsilon^2)(d+log(1/δ))/(1024ε2) labels. That is the floor of the fundamental theorem, with C1=1/1024C_1 = 1/1024C1​=1/1024.

from math import log, sqrt

def floor_log(eps, delta):
    return log(1 / (4 * delta)) / (2 * eps**2)
def floor_d(eps, d):
    return d / (512 * eps**2)
markov = (1 / 4 - 1 / 8) / (1 - 1 / 8)
print(round(markov, 4), round(1 / (8 * sqrt(2)), 4))
eps, delta, d = 0.05, 0.05, 100
print(round(floor_log(eps, delta)), round(floor_d(eps, d)),
      round((d + log(1 / delta)) / (1024 * eps**2)))

It prints 0.1429 0.0884, the 1/71/71/7 and the largest allowed ε\varepsilonε, then 322 78 40: for a class with d=100d = 100d=100 at ε=δ=0.05\varepsilon = \delta = 0.05ε=δ=0.05, the confidence floor is 322 labels, the dimension floor 78, and the combined formula 40, weaker than either, the price of one tidy formula. For the certificate’s ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1, the dimension part does not apply (0.1 is above 0.088), but the confidence floor of 80.47 does.

The ceiling with clean labels: ε\varepsilonε-nets

### Catching every bad hypothesis

Now the clean line. Some interval c∈Hc \in \mathcal Hc∈H is perfect, and ERM returns a hypothesis with no mistakes on SSS. When could that hypothesis still be bad?

Identify each hypothesis with the set of messages it calls junk. A hypothesis hhh disagrees with the truth ccc on the mistake region h △ c={x:h(x)≠c(x)}h \,\triangle\, c = \{x : h(x) \neq c(x)\}h△c={x:h(x)=c(x)}, the symmetric difference of the two sets: messages in exactly one of them. Its true risk is the probability mass of that region, LD(h)=D(h △ c)L_{\mathcal D}(h) = \mathcal D(h \,\triangle\, c)LD​(h)=D(h△c), where D(⋅)\mathcal D(\cdot)D(⋅) now means the chance that a fresh message lands in the set.

[diagram:symmetric-difference: built on the lesson page]

A bad hypothesis, with true risk at least ε\varepsilonε, has a mistake region of mass at least ε\varepsilonε. If even one training message falls in that region, the hypothesis makes a mistake on SSS, and ERM will not pick it. So ERM is safe as soon as the training messages hit every heavy mistake region. With noisy labels we needed every hypothesis’s score to be accurate; with clean labels, we only need every heavy region to be hit. That is a much weaker demand, and it is why the rate improves from 1/ε21/\varepsilon^21/ε2 to 1/ε1/\varepsilon1/ε.

Here is the idea for plain intervals of scores, with scores uniform on [0,1][0, 1][0,1]. Every interval of length at least ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1 must contain a training score. That fails exactly when two neighbouring scores (or a score and an end of [0,1][0,1][0,1]) are 0.1 or more apart. How many random scores do you need before that becomes rare?

import random

def is_eps_net(points, eps):
    xs = [0.0] + sorted(points) + [1.0]
    return max(b - a for a, b in zip(xs, xs[1:])) < eps
rng, eps, trials = random.Random(3), 0.1, 10_000
for m in (20, 50, 100):
    hits = sum(is_eps_net([rng.random() for _ in range(m)], eps)
               for _ in range(trials))
    print(m, round(hits / trials, 3))

It prints 20 0.007, 50 0.755 and 100 0.997: with 100 scores, all heavy intervals are hit 99.7% of the time.

### The definition

Definition (ε\varepsilonε-net). Let R\mathcal RR be a class of subsets of X\mathcal XX and D\mathcal DD a distribution over X\mathcal XX. A sequence of points SSS is an ε\varepsilonε-net for R\mathcal RR with respect to D\mathcal DD if

∀r∈R:D(r)≥ε  ⇒  r∩S≠∅.\forall r \in \mathcal R: \quad \mathcal D(r) \ge \varepsilon \;\Rightarrow\; r \cap S \neq \emptyset.∀r∈R:D(r)≥ε⇒r∩S=∅.

∀\forall∀ reads “for every”, D(r)\mathcal D(r)D(r) is the mass of the set rrr, the arrow ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ reads “implies”, and r∩S≠∅r \cap S \neq \emptysetr∩S=∅ says that at least one point of SSS lies in rrr (∅\emptyset∅ is the empty set). In plain words: every heavy set in the class contains at least one of the points. In the snippet, is_eps_net tests exactly this for intervals: every gap shorter than 0.1 means no interval of mass 0.1 fits between the points. Shattering and VC dimension make sense for any class of sets, by treating a set as the hypothesis that says 1 on it.

### The ε\varepsilonε-net theorem

The ε\varepsilonε-net theorem. Let R\mathcal RR have VC dimension d≥1d \ge 1d≥1, let ε,δ∈(0,1)\varepsilon, \delta \in (0, 1)ε,δ∈(0,1), and let

m≥8ε(2dlog⁡(16eε)+log⁡(2δ)).m \ge \frac{8}{\varepsilon} \left( 2d \log\left(\frac{16e}{\varepsilon}\right) + \log\left(\frac{2}{\delta}\right) \right).m≥ε8​(2dlog(ε16e​)+log(δ2​)).

Then, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over S∼DmS \sim \mathcal D^mS∼Dm, SSS is an ε\varepsilonε-net for R\mathcal RR.

The bracket has the VC dimension times a log of 1/ε1/\varepsilon1/ε, plus the log of 2/δ2/\delta2/δ, and the whole is multiplied by 8/ε8/\varepsilon8/ε, not divided by ε2\varepsilon^2ε2. In plain words: about 16dlog⁡(16e/ε)/ε16 d \log(16e/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon16dlog(16e/ε)/ε random points, plus a confidence term, hit every heavy set of a class of VC dimension ddd. For intervals at ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1, δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05, that is 2,239.2 points.

The proof has the same skeleton as the uniform-convergence proof in lesson 6b: a ghost sample, then a swap. Let BBB be the bad event “SSS is not an ε\varepsilonε-net”: some r∈Rr \in \mathcal Rr∈R has D(r)≥ε\mathcal D(r) \ge \varepsilonD(r)≥ε and contains no point of SSS. Draw a ghost sample T∼DmT \sim \mathcal D^mT∼Dm, independent of SSS, that nobody ever collects, and let B′B'B′ be the event “some r∈Rr \in \mathcal Rr∈R has D(r)≥ε\mathcal D(r) \ge \varepsilonD(r)≥ε, contains no point of SSS, and contains more than εm/2\varepsilon m/2εm/2 points of TTT”, counting points of TTT with repetition.

Claim 1. If εm≥8\varepsilon m \ge 8εm≥8, then P[B]≤2 P[B′]\mathbb P[B] \le 2\,\mathbb P[B']P[B]≤2P[B′].

The idea: a heavy set that SSS missed is very likely to be hit often by TTT, because it is heavy.

Proof. B′B'B′ can only happen when BBB does, so, averaging first over TTT for a fixed SSS (allowed because SSS and TTT are independent),

P[B′]=ES[1[S∈B]⋅PT[(S,T)∈B′]].\mathbb P[B'] = \mathbb E_{S}\Big[ \mathbb 1[S \in B] \cdot \mathbb P_{T}\big[(S, T) \in B'\big] \Big].P[B′]=ES​[1[S∈B]⋅PT​[(S,T)∈B′]].

Fix an SSS in BBB, and pick one witness rSr_SrS​: a set with mass p=D(rS)≥εp = \mathcal D(r_S) \ge \varepsilonp=D(rS​)≥ε that SSS misses. If TTT puts more than εm/2\varepsilon m/2εm/2 points in rSr_SrS​, then (S,T)(S, T)(S,T) is in B′B'B′. The number XXX of points of TTT in rSr_SrS​ is a sum of mmm independent coins with success chance ppp: mean pmpmpm, variance mp(1−p)mp(1-p)mp(1−p). Since pm/2≥εm/2pm/2 \ge \varepsilon m/2pm/2≥εm/2, it suffices that X>pm/2X > pm/2X>pm/2. By Chebyshev’s inequality (lesson 4: a quantity is at least ttt away from its mean with probability at most its variance over t2t^2t2),

P[X≤pm/2]≤P[∣X−pm∣≥pm/2]≤mp(1−p)(pm/2)2=4(1−p)pm<4εm≤12.\mathbb P[X \le pm/2] \le \mathbb P\big[|X - pm| \ge pm/2\big] \le \frac{mp(1-p)}{(pm/2)^2} = \frac{4(1 - p)}{pm} < \frac{4}{\varepsilon m} \le \frac12.P[X≤pm/2]≤P[∣X−pm∣≥pm/2]≤(pm/2)2mp(1−p)​=pm4(1−p)​<εm4​≤21​.

So PT[(S,T)∈B′]≥12\mathbb P_T[(S, T) \in B'] \ge \frac12PT​[(S,T)∈B′]≥21​ for every SSS in BBB, and P[B′]≥12P[B]\mathbb P[B'] \ge \frac12 \mathbb P[B]P[B′]≥21​P[B]. ■\blacksquare■

from math import comb

def lower_tail(m, p):
    return sum(comb(m, k) * p**k * (1 - p)**(m - k)
               for k in range(m + 1) if k <= p * m / 2)
for m, p in ((80, 0.1), (80, 0.3), (200, 0.1)):
    print(m, p, round(lower_tail(m, p), 4),
          round(4 * (1 - p) / (p * m), 4))

It prints

80 0.1 0.088 0.45
80 0.3 0.0015 0.1167
200 0.1 0.0081 0.18

The exact chance that a set of mass ppp gets at most half its expected share of TTT, next to Chebyshev’s bound. At εm=8\varepsilon m = 8εm=8 (first row) the bound is 0.45, just under one half, which is all Claim 1 needs; the truth is 0.088.

Claim 2 (the swap). P[B′]≤τR(2m) e−εm/4\mathbb P[B'] \le \tau_{\mathcal R}(2m) \, e^{-\varepsilon m/4}P[B′]≤τR​(2m)e−εm/4, where τR\tau_{\mathcal R}τR​ is the growth function.

The idea is lesson 6b’s: put all 2m2m2m points in one row, SSS first and TTT second. Because they are i.i.d., any other way of splitting the row into two halves of mmm is equally likely to have produced it. And for a set that holds many of the 2m2m2m points, it is very unlikely that a random half avoids all of them.

[diagram:ghost-swap: built on the lesson page]

Proof. Write the row as U=(u1,…,u2m)U = (u_1, \dots, u_{2m})U=(u1​,…,u2m​), with SSS the first mmm entries. Let α=εm/2\alpha = \varepsilon m/2α=εm/2. If (S,T)∈B′(S, T) \in B'(S,T)∈B′, some rrr misses the first half and holds more than α\alphaα of the 2m2m2m points (all of them in the second half). Forget the condition D(r)≥ε\mathcal D(r) \ge \varepsilonD(r)≥ε; this only makes the event larger. What matters about rrr is only which positions of the row it contains, its pattern, and the class produces at most τR(2m)\tau_{\mathcal R}(2m)τR​(2m) distinct patterns on 2m2m2m points. By the union bound over patterns,

P[B′]≤EU[∑patterns P of R on U1[∣P∣≥α]⋅1[P misses the first half]].\mathbb P[B'] \le \mathbb E_{U} \left[ \sum_{\text{patterns } P \text{ of } \mathcal R \text{ on } U} \mathbb 1\big[|P| \ge \alpha\big] \cdot \mathbb 1\big[P \text{ misses the first half}\big] \right].P[B′]≤EU​​patterns P of R on U∑​1[∣P∣≥α]⋅1[P misses the first half]​.

The sum runs over the distinct patterns, ∣P∣|P|∣P∣ counts the positions in a pattern, and each term is 1 for a heavy pattern that the first half misses. In plain words: the bad event needs at least one heavy pattern to dodge SSS completely, and we add up the chances pattern by pattern.

Now the swap. The entries of UUU are i.i.d., so permuting them gives a row with the same distribution, and the set of patterns and their sizes do not care about order. So the expectation is unchanged if “the first half” is replaced by any fixed set of mmm positions JJJ, and hence also by a uniformly random JJJ among all (2mm)\binom{2m}{m}(m2m​) of them. For a fixed row and a pattern with n=∣P∣≥αn = |P| \ge \alphan=∣P∣≥α positions, the chance that a random JJJ avoids all nnn of them is the chance of drawing mmm balls from a bag of 2m2m2m without touching any of nnn red ones:

(2m−nm)(2mm)=∏k=0m−12m−n−k2m−k≤(1−n2m)m≤(1−ε4)m≤e−εm/4.\frac{\binom{2m - n}{m}}{\binom{2m}{m}} = \prod_{k=0}^{m-1} \frac{2m - n - k}{2m - k} \le \left(1 - \frac{n}{2m}\right)^m \le \left(1 - \frac{\varepsilon}{4}\right)^m \le e^{-\varepsilon m/4}.(m2m​)(m2m−n​)​=k=0∏m−1​2m−k2m−n−k​≤(1−2mn​)m≤(1−4ε​)m≤e−εm/4.

The product draws the balls one at a time: the kkk-th draw avoids the red balls with chance 1−n/(2m−k)≤1−n/(2m)1 - n/(2m - k) \le 1 - n/(2m)1−n/(2m−k)≤1−n/(2m). Then n≥α=εm/2n \ge \alpha = \varepsilon m/2n≥α=εm/2 gives n/(2m)≥ε/4n/(2m) \ge \varepsilon/4n/(2m)≥ε/4, and 1−x≤e−x1 - x \le e^{-x}1−x≤e−x finishes. In plain words: a random half of the row dodges every one of εm/2\varepsilon m/2εm/2 marked points with chance at most e−εm/4e^{-\varepsilon m/4}e−εm/4. Each of the at most τR(2m)\tau_{\mathcal R}(2m)τR​(2m) patterns contributes at most this much, which proves the claim. ■\blacksquare■

from math import comb, exp

def miss_all(m, n):
    return comb(2 * m - n, m) / comb(2 * m, m)
m, eps = 100, 0.1
n = round(eps * m / 2)
print(n, f"{miss_all(m, n):.4f}", f"{(1 - n / (2*m))**m:.4f}",
      f"{exp(-eps * m / 4):.4f}")

It prints 5 0.0297 0.0795 0.0821: with 200 points and 5 marked, a random half dodges all five with chance 0.0297, under both bounds.

Completing the proof. Claims 1 and 2 and Sauer’s lemma (τR(2m)≤(2em/d)d\tau_{\mathcal R}(2m) \le (2em/d)^dτR​(2m)≤(2em/d)d) give

P[S is not an ε-net]≤2(2emd)de−εm/4.\mathbb P[S \text{ is not an } \varepsilon\text{-net}] \le 2 \left(\frac{2em}{d}\right)^d e^{-\varepsilon m/4}.P[S is not an ε-net]≤2(d2em​)de−εm/4.

We need this to be at most δ\deltaδ, that is, εm/4≥dlog⁡(2em/d)+log⁡(2/δ)\varepsilon m/4 \ge d \log(2em/d) + \log(2/\delta)εm/4≥dlog(2em/d)+log(2/δ). Use the tangent-line lemma with x=2em/dx = 2em/dx=2em/d and t=16e/εt = 16e/\varepsilont=16e/ε: dlog⁡(2em/d)≤dlog⁡(16/ε)+εm/8d\log(2em/d) \le d\log(16/\varepsilon) + \varepsilon m/8dlog(2em/d)≤dlog(16/ε)+εm/8. So it is enough that εm/8≥dlog⁡(16/ε)+log⁡(2/δ)\varepsilon m/8 \ge d\log(16/\varepsilon) + \log(2/\delta)εm/8≥dlog(16/ε)+log(2/δ), that is, m≥8ε(dlog⁡(16/ε)+log⁡(2/δ))m \ge \frac{8}{\varepsilon}(d \log(16/\varepsilon) + \log(2/\delta))m≥ε8​(dlog(16/ε)+log(2/δ)). The mmm in the theorem is larger than this, since 2dlog⁡(16e/ε)>dlog⁡(16/ε)2d\log(16e/\varepsilon) > d\log(16/\varepsilon)2dlog(16e/ε)>dlog(16/ε), so it qualifies. It also gives εm≥16dlog⁡(16e)>8\varepsilon m \ge 16 d\log(16e) > 8εm≥16dlog(16e)>8, as Claim 1 required. ■\blacksquare■

from math import e, exp, log

def failure_bound(m, eps, d):
    return 2 * (2 * e * m / d)**d * exp(-eps * m / 4)
def m_net(eps, delta, d):
    return 8 / eps * (2 * d * log(16 * e / eps) + log(2 / delta))
d, eps, delta = 2, 0.1, 0.05
print(round(m_net(eps, delta, d), 1))
for m in (500, 1_000, 2_240):
    print(m, f"{failure_bound(m, eps, d):.2g}")

It prints 2239.2, then 500 14, 1000 0.00021 and 2240 3.5e-17. At 500 points the bound is 14, which says nothing (a probability is at most 1); at 2,240 it is astronomically small. The theorem’s mmm is generous, but it is what we proved, and a certificate quotes what was proved.

### From nets to learning

One gap remains. The ε\varepsilonε-net theorem is about a class of sets, and we need it for the mistake regions h △ ch \,\triangle\, ch△c. Let Hc={h △ c:h∈H}\mathcal H_c = \{h \,\triangle\, c : h \in \mathcal H\}Hc​={h△c:h∈H}, the class of all mistake regions against the truth ccc.

Does Hc\mathcal H_cHc​ have the same VC dimension as H\mathcal HH? Yes, and the reason is a bijection again. On a finite set CCC, a pattern PPP of H\mathcal HH becomes the pattern P △ (c∩C)P \,\triangle\, (c \cap C)P△(c∩C) of Hc\mathcal H_cHc​: flip membership exactly at the points where ccc says junk. Flipping twice undoes it, so this is a bijection between the patterns of the two classes on CCC. They produce the same number of patterns on every set, so they shatter the same sets and have the same VC dimension.

m = 6
cuts = [c - 0.5 for c in range(m + 1)]
H_C = {tuple(int(a < x < b) for x in range(m))
       for a in cuts for b in cuts if a <= b}
c = (0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0)
H_c = {tuple(h_i ^ c_i for h_i, c_i in zip(h, c)) for h in H_C}
print(len(H_C), len(H_c), (1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0) in H_c)

It prints 22 22 True. The operator ^ is exclusive or, the symmetric difference on bits. Intervals make 22 patterns on six points, and so do their mistake regions against ccc, even though a mistake region need not be an interval: (1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0) is the region of the interval covering the first four points, which overshoots ccc by one message, and an interval that overshoots ccc on both sides leaves a region in two pieces.

The ceiling with clean labels. Let H\mathcal HH have VC dimension ddd, let D\mathcal DD be a distribution over X\mathcal XX, and let the labels come from some c∈Hc \in \mathcal Hc∈H. For ε,δ∈(0,1)\varepsilon, \delta \in (0,1)ε,δ∈(0,1) and mmm as in the ε\varepsilonε-net theorem, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ every ERM hypothesis has LD(h)<εL_{\mathcal D}(h) < \varepsilonLD​(h)<ε. Hence

mH(ε,δ)≤8ε(2dlog⁡(16eε)+log⁡(2δ)).m_{\mathcal H}(\varepsilon, \delta) \le \frac{8}{\varepsilon}\left( 2d \log\left(\frac{16e}{\varepsilon}\right) + \log\left(\frac{2}{\delta}\right) \right).mH​(ε,δ)≤ε8​(2dlog(ε16e​)+log(δ2​)).

Proof. By the ε\varepsilonε-net theorem for Hc\mathcal H_cHc​, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, SSS is an ε\varepsilonε-net for Hc\mathcal H_cHc​. On that event, take any hhh with LD(h)=D(h △ c)≥εL_{\mathcal D}(h) = \mathcal D(h \,\triangle\, c) \ge \varepsilonLD​(h)=D(h△c)≥ε: some training message lies in h △ ch \,\triangle\, ch△c, so hhh makes a mistake on SSS, and LS(h)>0L_S(h) > 0LS​(h)>0. But ccc itself has LS(c)=0L_S(c) = 0LS​(c)=0, so ERM returns a hypothesis with empirical risk 0, and that hypothesis cannot be such an hhh. Hence its true risk is below ε\varepsilonε. ■\blacksquare■

In plain words: with this many clean labels, every hypothesis consistent with them is good, because every bad one was caught red-handed. The shape is (dlog⁡(1/ε)+log⁡(1/δ))/ε(d\log(1/\varepsilon) + \log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon(dlog(1/ε)+log(1/δ))/ε up to constants (for ε≤1/2\varepsilon \le 1/2ε≤1/2, where log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon)log(1/ε) is at least log⁡2\log 2log2 and can absorb the constant log⁡(16e)\log(16e)log(16e)), which is exactly the realizable ceiling of the fundamental theorem.

The majority vote, as code

The floor proofs introduced one learner, the majority vote, and showed it is the best possible in the ddd-coin worlds. Here it is with the game that evaluates it.

MajorityVote(S, d):
  votes ← array of d zeros
  for each example (i, y) in S:
    votes[i] ← votes[i] + (1 if y = 1 else −1)
  for i = 1..d:
    if votes[i] > 0: guess[i] ← 1
    else if votes[i] < 0: guess[i] ← 0
    else: guess[i] ← a fair coin flip
  return guess

EstimationError(guess, b, ρ):
  wrong ← number of i with guess[i] ≠ b[i]
  return ρ · wrong / d

Here an example is written (i,y)(i, y)(i,y): the index iii of the shattered message it landed on, and its label. MajorityVote reads each example once and keeps one counter per message: O(m+d)O(m + d)O(m+d) time and O(d)O(d)O(d) space. EstimationError is O(d)O(d)O(d). The exact failure rate of the vote on one message with nnn labels, which the floor proofs bound from below, is a sum over the n+1n + 1n+1 possible counts of wrong labels: O(n)O(n)O(n) terms. For the two-world game it is the exact_fail function above.

Build it yourself. Using only the Python standard library:

def majority_vote(S, d, rng): ...
def estimation_error(guess, b, rho): ...
def exact_point_error(n, rho): ...
def coin_floor(n, rho): ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    assert majority_vote(S, d, random.Random(0)) == [1, 1, 0]
    err = estimation_error([1, 1, 0], (1, 0, 1), rho)
    assert abs(err - rho * 2 / 3) < 1e-12
    assert exact_point_error(0, rho) == 0.5
    assert round(exact_point_error(3, rho), 4) == 0.352
    assert all(exact_point_error(n, r) >= coin_floor(n, r) - 1e-12
               for n in range(60) for r in (0.1, 0.3, 0.7))

Implement majority_vote (the pseudocode, ties broken with rng), estimation_error (the risk identity), exact_point_error(n, rho) (the majority vote’s exact chance of guessing one message wrong from nnn labels of bias ρ\rhoρ, counting a tie as one half), and coin_floor(n, rho), the overlap lemma’s 12(1−1−(1−ρ2)n)\frac12(1 - \sqrt{1 - (1 - \rho^2)^n})21​(1−1−(1−ρ2)n​).

Fix the bug

Back to the auditor. Here is everything we proved, for her numbers: intervals, d=2d = 2d=2, ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1, δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05.

from math import ceil, e, log

d, eps, delta = 2, 0.1, 0.05
floor = log(1 / (4 * delta)) / (2 * eps**2)
agnostic = (256 * d * log(256 / eps**2)
            + 64 * log(4 / delta)) / eps**2
realizable = 8 / eps * (2 * d * log(16 * e / eps)
                        + log(2 / delta))
print(ceil(floor), ceil(agnostic), ceil(realizable))

It prints 81 547743 2240. Read it as the auditor will.

  • Noisy line, floor: no learner can certify ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1 at δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05 with 80 labels or fewer. The current 500 is above the floor, so it is not ruled out.
  • Noisy line, ceiling: 547,743 labels are proved to be enough for ERM. The current 500 is in the band where nobody has a proof. Not certifiable.
  • Clean line, ceiling: 2,240 labels are proved to be enough. The current 76 is not certifiable either.

In the lab below, the certificate has both lines on sliders, and the company will pay for at most 600,000 labels in total. Before you move anything, answer one question: finance proposes cutting the noisy line to 60 labels to save money. What does the floor say about that? Then set a budget for each line that the auditor can sign.
