What people get wrong

“The ceiling is the number of labels you need.” The ceiling is the number of labels this proof can vouch for. The two-world game needs about 269 labels in truth, the proved floor says 81, and the proved ceiling for intervals says 547,743. The truth sits somewhere between the fences, and the fences are far apart because the proofs spend constants freely.

“The floor only applies to bad learners.” The floor applies to every learner, because the adversary picks the world after the learner is fixed. The majority vote, the best learner in those worlds, still misses more than δ\deltaδ of the time below the floor.

“Clean labels just make the same bound smaller.” They change the rate. With noise, the learner must estimate every hypothesis’s risk to within ε\varepsilonε, which costs 1/ε21/\varepsilon^21/ε2. Without noise, it only needs every heavy mistake region to be hit once, which costs 1/ε1/\varepsilon1/ε. At ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1 that is the difference between 2,240 and 547,743.

“The proof shows the theorem exactly as stated.” The noisy ceiling we proved has an extra log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon)log(1/ε) next to ddd. The theorem’s cleaner shape needs lesson 27’s chaining plus a covering bound for VC classes, which we did not prove.

Recap and the next bug

  1. The noisy ceiling: mistake patterns are as many as labellings, Sauer bounds them by (em/d)d(em/d)^d(em/d)d, Massart turns that into a Rademacher complexity of order dlog⁡(m)/m\sqrt{d\log(m)/m}dlog(m)/m​, and the generalization bound of lesson 26, applied to both signs of the loss, makes every hypothesis honest to within ε\varepsilonε once mmm is of order (dlog⁡(1/ε)+log⁡(1/δ))/ε2(d\log(1/\varepsilon) + \log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^2(dlog(1/ε)+log(1/δ))/ε2.
  2. The confidence floor: two worlds that differ only in the direction of one message, and the overlap lemma, show that every learner needs at least log⁡(1/(4δ))/(2ε2)\log(1/(4\delta))/(2\varepsilon^2)log(1/(4δ))/(2ε2) labels.
  3. The dimension floor: ddd shattered messages with hidden directions, averaged over all 2d2^d2d worlds, show that every learner needs at least d/(512ε2)d/(512\varepsilon^2)d/(512ε2) labels; the majority vote is the best learner there and still fails.
  4. The clean ceiling: an ε\varepsilonε-net hits every heavy mistake region, a ghost sample and a swap show that order (dlog⁡(1/ε)+log⁡(1/δ))/ε(d\log(1/\varepsilon) + \log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon(dlog(1/ε)+log(1/δ))/ε random points form one, and then every consistent hypothesis is good.
  5. Together: the fundamental theorem’s floor with C1=1/1024C_1 = 1/1024C1​=1/1024, its realizable ceiling, and its noisy ceiling up to a log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon)log(1/ε).

The auditor signs. You have barely put the certificate away when the product team walks in with a new plan. The filter will no longer sort mail into junk and keep: it will sort every message into one of hundreds of folders, invoices, newsletters, travel, receipts, each team’s project. A hypothesis now returns one of hundreds of labels, not two, and the VC dimension, which counts the ways to label points with 0 and 1, no longer applies. What replaces it? And which multiclass problems are learnable at all? That is the next lesson.

Concept check

Write your answers down before moving on to the next lesson, with your reasoning, not just the answer.

  1. In the confidence floor, the theorem requires ε<1/2\varepsilon < 1/\sqrt2ε<1/2​ and δ<1/4\delta < 1/4δ<1/4, and the proof builds its two worlds with a gap ε′\varepsilon'ε′ slightly larger than ε\varepsilonε. For each of these three choices, say which step of the proof would break without it.
  2. In the dimension floor, the learner sees the labels of all ddd messages, yet the proof treats each message as if only its own labels mattered. Why are the labels of the other messages useless for guessing the direction bib_ibi​? Which assumption about how bbb is chosen makes this true, and would the argument survive if the adversary always chose b=(1,1,…,1)b = (1, 1, \dots, 1)b=(1,1,…,1)?
